title: No Decline in Number of American Tobacco Smokers

content_html_sanitized:
The percentage of American adults who smoke tobacco has remained virtually unchanged during the 1990s.

The U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) said a 1995 U.S. survey of 17,213 adults found that 24.7 percent of them smoked. The agency estimated that 47 million adults nationwide were smokers and that 32 million of them want to quit.

The proportion of adults who smoke has been stuck around 25 percent since 1990 after falling from about 30 percent in 1985. Health officials had set a goal to cut the percentage of adult smokers nationwide to 15 percent by the year 2000.

The CDC said about 44.3 million adults have quit smoking. 70 percent of smokers who want to quit don't quit because  nicotine is a "very strong and persuasive drug" according to the CDC.

The CDC said that the number of teenagers who smoke is increasing steadily and many of them are smoking cigars as often as adults. The agency said earlier this year that one in four high school students had smoked a cigar during the past year.

Eriksen said that one of the reasons why cigarettes remain popular is their relatively low cost. "The price of cigarettes has actually gone down over time, compared to other products," he said.

Smoking rates have fallen markedly in California and Massachusetts, where excise taxes were imposed to fund education and prevention programs. In October, Dr. John Seffrin, the chief executive officer of the American Cancer Society, proposed a $2 tax on all tobacco products.

The American Cancer Society estimates that tobacco use causes more than 400,000 deaths every year, including 180,000 deaths from cardiovascular disease. The organization says smoking is responsible for 30 percent of all cancer deaths nationwide and more than 80 percent of lung cancers. Quitting for a year can cut in half the excess risk of heart disease caused by smoking.
